articles.title: The Road Trip Haunted By Pokémon Go And The Hit Game That Made A Summer Stranger
articles.subtitle: Donned in a leather hat, our ghost tour guide has told us not to worry. He had already altered the route through Salem to better accommodate “Pokémon trainers.” The crowd chuckled. I wasn’t underestimating the gravity of the situation. Not anymore.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Donned in a leather hat, our ghost tour guide has told us not to worry. He had already altered the route through Salem to better accommodate “Pokémon trainers.” The crowd chuckled. I wasn’t underestimating the gravity of the situation. Not anymore. It was July of 2016. Night three of Pokémon Go ’s unleashing. Night two of my road trip. My brother and I happened to be driving through New England, watching in real time as one one game transformed the use of public space.

Standing before the Gardner–Pingree House, where Captain Joseph White was murdered in 1830 by the Brothers Knapp, I asked my brother if Gengars were floating through the halls. Playing tag and slobbering all over the old naval specter. He told me the game wasn’t that sophisticated yet, and beyond identifying bodies of water the Pokémon were mostly a crapshoot.

Weaving through the quiet night, the guide pointed out landmarks of the grisly witch trials, the more ominous graves, and estates that hosted deaths that would inspire the likes of Edgar Allen Poe. All the while tourists glanced at their phone, scanning for Pokémon. Despite the reroute, a third peeled off and vanished before the tour ended. On most days that would be creepy.

Pokémon Go wasn’t available back home in Toronto. Niantic launched the game in the United States and Australia, while most of the world had to sit on their hands. But us hosers caught wind. Driving towards the Falls to cross the border, I was on the phone with Raina Douris, a radio host working on a piece about the game capturing our southern neighbors. I ran a primer on the game and augmented reality.

Fads like Foursquare were fresh enough in memory as a shorthand for geotagged playground games. Pokémon, prematurely labeled a fad in the late ‘90s, never went away, leaving space to gab.

“Pokémon are still really popular, not just with us millennials,” I told Douris. “There’s all kinds of Pokémon. There’s one that’s basically a horse on fire.”

Our goal was to bolt to a friend’s place in Boston for the first night, then curve through Maine and Vermont to French Canada. That meant the first day would be a cannonball run of a drive. Thankfully it was a breathtaking stretch. Even parallel to the Catskills, the forested length through New York state was lush in waves of foliage.

The radio call had nearly faded from my mind when we pulled up to grab some Wegmans snacks. With bags of sodas and Pop Tarts they don’t allow in Canada, I noticed something odd across the parking lot. Four young kids, eyes locked on their phone, perching on the steps of a small derelict church. Not talking. Not boarding. Almost ritualistic like focus and configuration.

Daylight was a memory by the time we arrived in Boston, and parking wasn’t any easier to find. Scanning the road for a spot, earlier foreshadowing evolved into something of a zombie film. We kept spotting packs of kids roaming in unusual places. Inspecting lane ways and YMCA dumpsters. Lured out into the world by the Pokémon Company. We generally had to accept this new reality as it increased through the trip.

From historical graveyards to seaside lobster pounds, dozens of kids seemingly being pied piper into the public. I suspect the only reason we didn’t come across any at the Battery Steele was a lack of reception.

Much like the video games it spun-off from, Pokémon Go has persevered. It’s also refined itself through a decade of user trends, the data from which might be used for less splendid applications. But it’s hard to top those first wild west days in an already surreal summer, where Hillary Clinton tried to do youth outreach with DOA puns and Pokémon trainers were accidentally Stand By Me -ing themselves with a ravine-side corpse or two.

articles.title: Lil Finder Guy pet was the gateway to building my own Mac apps with Codex
articles.subtitle: At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet. This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it?
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet.

This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it? My first real task with Codex was putting together a virtual Lil Finder Guy for fun.

A month later, I’m using two Mac apps that Codex built at my direction. Toying around with Codex Pets was the gateway for me to better understand its capabilities.

OpenAI tools for making apps have improved a lot since last summer

Both Mac apps are just for my use and not intended for distribution, but that’s just a choice and not a Codex limitation. They’re genuinely usable and useful software applications that serve my needs.

One tool is called Flow, and it just helps me track activity and changes around the App Store. Another offers a better experience with using a social network on the Mac without certain constraints of Chrome, like minimum window width.

The experience taught me just how much these tools have changed since this time last year as well.

For example, I wanted to make my own Launchpad replacement when macOS Tahoe removed the feature from the Mac last June. (Launchpad wasn’t for everyone, but it was part of my muscle memory since OS X Lion. I’ve since moved on from missing it.)

Using ChatGPT to walk me through Xcode while copying and pasting blocks of code and screenshots of errors was a process void of much joy. Even as a proof-of-concept, I couldn’t get the app that I was making to resemble the behavior that I had in mind. Nuking the project felt good.

With Codex, I had a functioning app that solved my specific need in almost no time (and literally no Xcode). I was able to go from idea to minimum viable software almost immediately. The rest of my first month with Codex and making the app was spent adding features beyond my original need and getting more specific about how things should look and behave.

There are more tools that I want to make for myself next, and having Codex’s capabilities on the Mac has been a real boost.

(Next, I’ll be watching Apple’s WWDC announcements with a new eye for what additional capabilities become available. I’m also cautious about any changes that may break my newfound system for turning ideas into functioning tools.)

Computer Use in Codex is a major unlock

Part of what makes Codex good at this compared to my experience using ChatGPT a year ago is that the model and app are made for coding and generally just doing things for you.

ChatGPT will absorb most or all of this functionality as a feature within the main app, but the extent of this remains to be seen. For now, there’s one thing in particular about Codex that made all the difference in the world: Computer Use.

Codex is far from the only coding agent available on the Mac, and it’s not the only version with a computer use feature either. But Codex’s Computer Use feature is phenomenal. On the Mac, it works in the background without taking over your machine. For me, this has meant I’ve been able to use my Mac, uninterrupted, while this coding agent expertly follows my direction.

Codex’s Computer Use essentially unlocks the complete opposite experience from what ChatGPT provided in this department last summer. Instead of it providing me with guidance and not much perspective, I’ve been able to guide it and vastly expand my own perspective.

You don’t have to spend a lot to get Codex experience

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.content:
Nintendo Nintendo Switch The Legend of Zelda

In stark contrast to the upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on the Nintendo Switch 2, a game that everyone in the world knew about before its official announcement, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom was such a secret that, according to two ex-PR leads, “less than 10 people” at Nintendo of America knew about it before it was announced at E3 2019.

This comes directly from former Nintendo of America PR managers Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang (via GamesRadar ), who are now perhaps better known by their YouTube handle Kit & Krysta. The two ex-Nintendo PR managers left Nintendo in 2022 and have been spilling info about the company’s inner workings on their YouTube channel ever since, but were, obviously, a lot better at keeping Nintendo’s secrets during their employment.

Case in point, according to the duo, “less than 10 people” at Nintendo of America were aware of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom’s existence before its trailer dropped at the final E3 in 2019.

Funnily enough, according to Ellis, even his own boss was not privy to the reveal, as the list of those who were informed of its announcement before it was revealed at E3 only consisted of “a couple of the Japan liaison people,” former Nintendo of America President Doug Bowser, of course, and Ellis.

According to Ellis, he was handpicked as one of the lucky few who were informed of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom’s existence due to his PR and marketing work on The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. Well, maybe “lucky” is the wrong word to use here, because as Ellis went on to reveal, the secretive nature of the project resulted in his workload massively increasing.

“Initially I thought, well, there’s not that much for me to do,” Ellis explained. “But, as we got closer and closer to [E3 2019] it became clear that I actually had a ton to do, because… y’know there was this big communications team–this E3 machine, cranking out materials[…]it became clear that I had to do all of these different teams’ jobs in secret.”

Even Yang humorously recalled that Ellis’ own boss was standing next to her during the games’ announcement, and was just as shocked as she was to see it for the first time. Personally, it’s kind of a shame that, in the age of video game leaks that we currently live in, we rarely get treated to big reveals like this anymore.

Just imagine how hype it would have been if we heard about Ocarina of Time’s remake for the first time at the Nintendo Direct it was officially revealed in, instead of via NateTheHate’s podcast.

articles.content:
Ahead of yesterday’s keynote, we asked you how optimistic you were about what the company was likely to announce. The executive summary was that there was absolutely no consensus.

Votes were split very evenly between very optimistic, somewhat optimistic and not very. So now that you’ve heard what Apple had to say, what were your impressions …?

We yesterday summarised the possible reasons for both optimism and pessimism. On the plus side, the new features are being powered by Google’s Gemini models, and these appear to be at least close to delivering on the promises made for them.

On the negative side is Apple’s track record to date, which started with a glossy ad promising lots of exciting AI features for the iPhone 16 and ended with having to make a U-turn on these and delete the video.

War for Westeros won't have the chance to redeem this franchise's video game reputation until early 2027

Related

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros has reemerged over a year after its announcement, although that also came with the news that it will now launch in 2027.

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros is a real-time strategy game based on the HBO show. The RTS title is being developed by PlaySide, the publisher of Mouse: P.I. For Hire, and was supposed to release this year. It has flown under the radar since its reveal during a crowded Summer Game Fest 2025 kickoff showcase, but attracted some attention again when a delay to "early 2027" was confirmed last week.

" War for Westeros will now launch in early 2027," PlaySide stated in a Steam blog post. "We remain unwavering in our mission to deliver a real-time strategy game set in the world of Westeros that meets the expectations of both RTS players and Game of Thrones fans. This decision gives us the time needed to continue building towards that goal and ensure that the game reaches the high level of quality we are aiming for."

Alongside the delay announcement, PlaySide's post features brief gameplay clips showcasing its factions, hero abilities, heavy cavalry units, and large maps. If you enjoy series like Total War, War for Westeros looks like it offers a similar RTS experience with Game of Thrones flair. If PlaySide can deliver, War for Westeros could easily become the best game based on this franchise yet.

Despite Game of Thrones' popularity as a franchise over the past decade, Warner Bros. has failed to properly capitalize on that in the video game medium. Telltale's oft-forgotten Game of Thrones title and Reigns: Game of Thrones were pretty good, but otherwise the series has been relegated mostly to mobile games that aren't for everyone.

While Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment is reportedly prioritizing Game of Thrones as a primary franchise going forward, War for Westeros should still launch long before whatever comes from that effort. While delays are sometimes disappointing, in War for Westeros ' case, it was actually a nice reminder that the game exists and is heading toward a full release on Windows PC in 2027.
